extraction.segment_function: The segment analyzes key concepts in Hannah Arendt's The Human Condition, specifically focusing on the category of process, its antithetical relation to human action, its characterization as a realm of necessity, and the role of homo faber and work in modernity.

claims.claim: Process is defined as the antithesis of action, functioning as a sequence of changes predetermined by an inner impersonal law operating as a cause-effect chain.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Process is the antithesis of action which needs free, undetermined human individuals being able to initiate new beginnings in the world. Process is the sequence of changes predetermined by an inner impersonal law regulating the order of these changes.

claims.claim: Modernity in its first phase is characterized by the victory of homo faber operating under means-end rationality to produce artificial things, an activity that inherently entails violence against nature.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Modernity, at least in its first phase, for her, means the victory of homo faber who, under the guidance of means-end rationality , began, in ever-increasing amount and speed, to produce large variety of artificial things. Homo faber seemed to become the master of the Earth who continuously expands the reach of his power over his environment. The activity of fabrication inherently entails the element of violence directed against lifeless and living nature.
qualifications: at least in its first phase

definitions.definition: The sequence of changes predetermined by an inner impersonal law regulating the order of these changes, characterized by fluidity, ephemerality, and futility as a terrain of necessity.

distinctions.distinction: Process is a sequence of changes predetermined by an inner impersonal law and terrain of necessity, whereas action needs free, undetermined human individuals able to initiate new beginnings.
